title: Lychee in Beer: Keeping a Fragile Aroma | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew with lychee: why its rose-like aroma fades, when to add the fruit, fresh versus canned and the light beers that let it show.
teaser: Lychee smells of roses and summer. It also disappears faster than any other fruit we brew with.
standfirst: Lychee is one of the hardest fruits to keep in a beer. Its floral aroma is delicate, volatile and easily scrubbed out by fermentation. Here is how to hold on to it.
sections: Lychee aroma is floral and fragile

The scent of a fresh lychee owes a lot to rose oxide and floral terpene alcohols such as geraniol and linalool. The same family of compounds gives Gewürztraminer wine its lychee note. They are small, volatile molecules. Heat drives them off. Rising CO2 during fermentation carries them out through the airlock.

That shapes every decision. Lychee rewards cold, late additions and punishes anything hot or early. A lychee beer brewed like a mango beer usually ends up tasting of faint sweetness and nothing else.

Never put lychee in the boil or the whirlpool. Add it after fermentation is complete, or very close to it, ideally once the beer has been cooled to 10 °C or below. Some brewers add the fruit and then hold at cellar temperature for three to five days before crashing.

Expect a small refermentation from the fruit sugar. Lychee is sweet, often 15 to 20 °Brix when ripe, so it adds a few points of gravity. If you add fruit cold, the yeast works slowly and less aroma is lost. Leave pressure release or an airlock in place, because sealed vessels with fresh fruit sugar can build pressure.

Fresh lychee season in India is short: May and June for the famous Shahi lychee of Muzaffarpur in Bihar, which holds a geographical indication tag, with Dehradun and parts of West Bengal not far behind. The fruit browns and loses aroma within days of picking.

Peel, stone and freeze the fruit the day you buy it. Freezing preserves aroma better than any cooking step. Canned lychee in syrup works too and is available all year. Weigh the fruit, drain the syrup and decide whether to add it: the syrup is mostly sugar and will push up the alcohol a little. Check the tin for preservatives, which can stall the yeast.

Because the aroma is gentle, lychee needs a higher rate than loud fruits like jackfruit. For a clear lychee character, start at 150 to 250 grams of peeled, stoned fruit per litre. A 20 litre batch at 200 g/L takes 4 kg of flesh, which is roughly 6 to 7 kg of whole fruit with skins and stones.

That ratio is the one floor detail worth remembering: the stone and skin are around a third of the weight of a lychee, so buy accordingly. Lightly crush the flesh rather than blending to a fine purée. It extracts well and is easier to rack off.

Lychee is sweet, so a heavy dose changes the strength of the beer more than most brewers expect. Check the juice on a refractometer before you add the fruit. Suppose it reads 18 °Brix.

At 200 grams of flesh per litre, the fruit brings about 36 grams of sugar per litre. That is roughly 3.6 °Plato, or 14 gravity points. Fermented out, it adds close to 1.8% ABV, a little less after the fruit's own water dilutes the beer. A 4.5% base beer finishes nearer 6%. That changes the balance, the label and how the beer drinks on a hot afternoon.

There are two ways to handle it. Brew the base beer lighter, around 1.036 to 1.040, so the finished beer lands where you want it. Or accept the extra strength and give the beer a little more body so it does not taste hot. Either way, take a gravity reading once the fruit fermentation has stopped and record it. Guessing the ABV of a fruit beer is how labels end up wrong.
Base beers that let lychee show

Lychee is easily buried, so the base beer must stay out of the way:

  • A Berliner weisse or light kettle sour, where acidity lifts the floral notes.
  • A clean pale lager or Kölsch-style ale, under 20 IBU.
  • A witbier, with very restrained coriander so the spice does not fight the fruit.
  • A hazy pale ale with a gentle, fruity hop such as a light dose of a tropical variety.

Skip roasted malt, crystal malt over about 5% and assertive hop bitterness. For a tea-and-lychee idea, our guide to brewing with tea shows how jasmine or green tea can carry the floral side further.

Even a well-made lychee beer fades faster than the base beer. Oxygen and warm storage strip the floral notes within weeks. Rack with as little splashing as possible, purge kegs and bottles with CO2 where you can and keep the finished beer cold. In an Indian summer, a lychee beer left at room temperature will taste flat long before it tastes stale.

Getting a fragile aroma from fruit to glass, through fermentation, conditioning and packaging, is exactly where fruit beers succeed or fail. That end-to-end view is what a style course builds.

Your first step: peel and freeze one kilo of lychee in season, then add it cold at 200 g/L to five litres of finished pale beer and taste on days three, five and seven.
faqs: Why does lychee aroma disappear from beer?
Its floral compounds are volatile. Heat drives them off and fermentation CO2 carries them out, so add lychee cold and late, after primary fermentation.
Can I use canned lychee for beer?
Yes. Drain and weigh the fruit, decide whether to add the syrup and check the tin for preservatives that could stall fermentation.
How much lychee goes into a 20 litre batch?
About 3 to 5 kg of peeled, stoned flesh, which is 150 to 250 grams per litre. Buy roughly half as much again in whole fruit.
